interviewQuestions.question: This product just launched and got a flash crowd of new users — how does your design cope?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd first ask whether this was a scheduled launch or an unpredictable viral spike, since that determines how much I can prepare versus how much has to be handled reactively. Either way, the core move is shedding load gracefully at the edge before it reaches the backend — a virtual waiting room admitting users at a controlled rate, so a flood becomes a predictable stream instead of an uncontrolled surge hitting the database directly.

For a scheduled launch, I'd add a gradual, feature-flagged rollout — 1% of users, then 10%, then 100%, watching metrics at each step — and pre-warm caches and connection pools before doors open, so the first wave of real users isn't also paying a cold-start cost.

I'd close by naming that the waiting room itself has to be the cheapest, most scalable thing I own, since it's now the component absorbing the whole surge.

**Testing:** whether you reach for admission control and staged rollout, not just 'autoscaling will handle it.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Coping with a launch flash crowd

interviewQuestions.question: The waiting room itself gets overwhelmed by the flash crowd — what protects that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is the recursive version of the single-point-of-failure question, and I'd treat it the same way: the waiting room has to be the cheapest, most horizontally-scalable thing in the whole system, since it's now absorbing the entire uncontrolled surge that everything else is protected from.

Concretely, that means it should do almost nothing per request — check a counter, maybe set a cookie identifying queue position — rather than anything requiring a database lookup or heavy computation. If it did real work per visitor, I'd just have moved the bottleneck one hop earlier instead of solving it. I'd also make sure it scales independently and trivially, since it's the one component explicitly designed to face unbounded load.

**Testing:** whether you follow the SPOF-elimination mindset all the way through to your own fix, instead of assuming the fix is immune to the problem it solves.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Protecting the waiting room itself

interviewQuestions.question: How do you know your flash-crowd handling is actually working, in real time, during the launch?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd name the specific dashboards I'd have open live, not just say I'm 'monitoring it.' Admission rate versus backend capacity — am I letting people in faster than the backend can actually serve them. Backend error rate and latency — is admitted traffic succeeding, or is the backend already straining. Queue depth and estimated wait time — is the line growing faster than it's draining, which would mean my admission rate is set too high or too low relative to actual capacity.

I'd treat 'it's working' as those numbers staying within planned bounds, not a vibe — and I'd have the ability to throttle the admission rate down immediately, live, if the backend metrics start moving the wrong way.

**Testing:** whether you can name concrete, actionable signals instead of a vague sense that things seem fine.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Verifying it's working in real time
